result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.transform_with_spanner()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Transform graph to a spanner with given stretch. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L16429-L16555){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.transform_with_spanner( stretch, weight=None, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Spanner](/assets/graphs/transform-with-spanner.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node ladder with two diagonal shortcuts, A to E and B to F, in the accent color. The stretch-2 spanner drops both diagonals, shown dashed: each one is replaced by a two-step path, so no distance more than doubles." width="100%"} A spanner is a sparse subgraph that approximates distances in the original graph. For any pair of nodes `u` and `v`, the distance in the spanner is at most `stretch=` times the distance in the original graph: `distance_spanner(u, v) ≤ stretch × distance_original(u, v)` The resulting spanner preserves approximate distances while using fewer edges, making it useful for graph compression, network backbone extraction, and approximate distance queries. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [stretch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum distance approximation factor. Must be ≥ `1.0`. Lower `stretch=` values give better approximations but more edges. Higher `stretch=` values create sparser spanners. [weight]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edge attribute to use as distance/weight. If `None`, all edges have weight `1` (unweighted graph). [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducibility. The algorithm has randomized components, so different seeds may produce different spanners with the same stretch guarantee. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with the same nodes but a subset of edges that forms a spanner with the specified stretch. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If stretch < `1.0` or if graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A $t$-spanner is a subgraph $H \subseteq G$ that preserves every pairwise distance up to a multiplicative factor: $d_H(u, v) \le t \cdot d_G(u, v)$ for all node pairs. This implementation uses a greedy scan that considers edges in weight order and admits each one only when the current spanner cannot already reach its endpoints within the stretch bound, costing $O(mn)$ time. The Baswana-Sen (2007) randomized algorithm attains the same guarantee in expected linear time with a tighter sparsity bound but is trickier to implement. The greedy variant here is chosen for clarity and determinism up to the tie-breaking controlled by `seed=`. For unweighted graphs the resulting spanner holds $O(n^{1 + 1/k})$ edges with $k = \lfloor(t + 1)/2\rfloor$, which is optimal assuming the Erdős girth conjecture. Weighted graphs may keep more edges but still dramatically fewer than the original. Spanners are the workhorse behind graph compression, network-backbone extraction, and fast approximate distance queries, and they make an excellent preprocessing step before running an expensive shortest-path or diameter computation. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 5-cycle, a 2-spanner can skip some edges while still guaranteeing every shortest path stretches by at most a factor of `2`: ::: {#87ef5ce6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() for i in range(5): g.add_node(label=str(i)) # Create a cycle for i in range(5): g.add_edge(source=str(i), target=str((i+1) % 5)) spanner = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=2.0) spanner.count_edges() < g.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Weighted graphs work the same way -- here a costly direct edge can be dropped if a cheaper indirect route still satisfies the stretch bound: ::: {#f626b070 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=1.0) g.add_edge(source="B", target="C", weight=1.0) g.add_edge(source="A", target="C", weight=5.0) spanner = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=3.0, weight="weight") spanner.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Raising `stretch=` trades approximation accuracy for sparsity -- on a random graph, a looser stretch bound consistently produces fewer edges: ::: {#e30350f6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph() g.add_gnp_graph(n=50, p=0.1, seed=23) original_edges = g.count_edges() spanner2 = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=2.0, seed=23) spanner3 = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=3.0, seed=23) spanner3.count_edges() < spanner2.count_edges() < original_edges ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: :::
